- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

content.text:
r02.

The premise is incorrect: **there is no per-user API rate-limiting middleware in this repository.** No rate-limiter, throttle, or request-count limit is registered anywhere in the request path, so there are no "request limits" to report.

What actually exists:

**The API interceptor chain** is registered in `server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-141` for the Connect/gRPC API:
```go
connectInterceptors := connect.WithInterceptors(
    NewMetadataInterceptor(),      // Convert HTTP headers to gRPC metadata first
    NewLoggingInterceptor(logStacktraces),
    NewRecoveryInterceptor(logStacktraces),
    NewAuthInterceptor(authorizer),
)
```
These four interceptors — metadata, logging, panic recovery, and authentication — are the complete middleware set (defined in `server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go`). **None of them performs rate limiting.**

The only request-bounding control is a **request body size limit**, not a rate limit: `maxAPIRequestBytes = 256 << 20` (256 MiB), applied via `http.MaxBytesHandler` and `connect.WithReadMaxBytes` at `server/router/api/v1/v1.go:20, 126, 141, 144`. This caps how large a single request can be, not how many requests a user may make.

The only mention of "rate limiting" in the codebase is documentation/example text, not implemented code:
- `internal/email/doc.go:86` — a comment suggesting email sending *could* be rate-limited.
- `internal/email/README.md:286-295` — an example snippet showing how one *might* add `golang.org/x/time/rate` for email (10 emails/sec), presented as a suggestion, not wired into anything.

So if you're looking for per-user API rate limiting with configured request limits, it does not exist here; the API relies on authentication/authorization plus a 256 MiB body-size cap instead.


## 3 & 4. What actually exists instead

There are no request-per-time-window limits anywhere. The only "limit"-style protections are:

**A. Concurrency semaphores (global, not per-user; caps in-flight work, not request rate)** — `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:39-60`
```go
thumbnailSemaphore:       semaphore.NewWeighted(3), // 3 concurrent thumbnail generations
imageProcessingSemaphore: semaphore.NewWeighted(2), // 2 concurrent image (EXIF strip) ops
```
The image semaphore is acquired in `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service.go:158-160`; on failure it returns `codes.ResourceExhausted, "too many image processing requests"`. The acquire/release helper is `acquireImageProcessingSlot` at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/attachment_service_image.go:67-77`. These use `golang.org/x/sync/semaphore` (concurrency gating), not a time-windowed rate limiter, and are process-global rather than per user.

**B. Request body size limits** — `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:126,141,144` wrap handlers in `http.MaxBytesHandler(..., maxAPIRequestBytes)` and `connect.WithReadMaxBytes(maxAPIRequestBytes)`. This caps payload size, not request frequency.

**Email "rate limit" is only a documentation recommendation, not implemented** — `/bench/repo/internal/email/doc.go:86` lists "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" under Security Considerations, but there is no corresponding implementation in `/bench/repo/internal/email/`.

**No reverse-proxy/gateway rate-limit config** is shipped in the repo. There are no nginx/Caddy/Traefik config files with `limit_req` or equivalent; the only reference to reverse proxies is `/bench/repo/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml:88` (a dropdown asking which proxy the user runs). The `internal/scheduler/middleware.go` "middleware" is for background job handlers (Recovery/Logging/Timeout), not HTTP/API requests.

### Bottom line
Rate limiting is effectively **not implemented**. Abuse mitigation relies on (a) global concurrency semaphores for image/thumbnail processing, (b) max request-body sizes, and (c) batch-size argument caps. If per-user API rate limiting is a requirement, it would need to be added — the natural insertion point is a new Connect interceptor in the chain at `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go:133-138` and/or an Echo middleware at `/bench/repo/server/server.go:51-52`.</result>
